title: Strict mode versus sloppy mode
hook: Strict mode is a opt-in subset of JavaScript that turns silent mistakes into thrown errors. Modules and classes run in strict mode automatically — sloppy-mode footguns still appear in legacy scripts and interview trick questions.

blocks.text: JavaScript originally allowed many error-prone patterns: assigning to undeclared variables created globals, duplicate parameter names were legal, and `delete` on non-configurable properties failed silently. Strict mode (`'use strict'` or ES modules) opts into stricter rules: assignments to undeclared bindings throw ReferenceError, `delete` on non-configurable properties throws, `eval` does not introduce variables into surrounding scope, and `this` in plain functions is `undefined` instead of the global object. Sloppy mode is the legacy default for classic scripts without the directive. C# has no equivalent toggle — the language always enforces definite assignment, no accidental globals, and compile-time errors for most strict-mode catches in JavaScript.

entries.plainDefinition: A restricted variant of JavaScript that throws on actions that were silent errors in sloppy mode.
entries.example: `'use strict'; x = 1;` throws if `x` was never declared.

entries.plainDefinition: The default behavior for classic scripts without `'use strict'`. More permissive and error-prone.
entries.example: In sloppy mode, `mistyped = 5` can create a global variable.

entries.plainDefinition: A variable created by assignment without `var`/`let`/`const` in sloppy mode, polluting the global object.
entries.example: `function f() { oops = 1; }` adds `oops` to `window` in browsers.

blocks.text: Production bundles almost always run in strict mode — ES modules are strict by default, and bundlers inject the directive. Interview questions still test sloppy behavior because legacy codebases and inline scripts exist. Strict mode changes `this` binding in functions, forbids `with`, and makes `arguments` not alias parameters — bugs that only appear when mixing modes. TypeScript can flag some issues at compile time, but `noImplicitAny` does not catch implicit globals in emitted sloppy scripts. C# never lets you assign to an undeclared identifier; treat strict mode as JavaScript catching up partially to that safety.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: Strict mode: no implicit globals, `this` is `undefined` in plain functions, duplicate params illegal, `delete` throws on non-configurable. Modules are always strict.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: File-level directive
items.body: `'use strict';` as the first statement in a script or function body enables strict mode for that scope and nested functions.

items.title: ES modules
items.body: Any file parsed as `type="module"` or `import`/`export` syntax is automatically strict — no directive needed.

items.title: Class bodies
items.body: Methods and constructors inside `class` run in strict mode even in a sloppy script file.

items.title: Cannot escape
items.body: Strict mode does not leak outward — a sloppy outer function can contain a strict inner function, but not vice versa for the outer scope.

diagram.title: Strict vs sloppy decision tree

snippet.label: Implicit global vs strict error
snippet.explanation: Sloppy mode assigns to an undeclared name on the global object. Strict mode throws immediately — similar to C# refusing an undeclared identifier at compile time.

snippet.label: this in plain functions
snippet.explanation: Strict mode sets `this` to `undefined` for unbound function calls. In C#, instance methods without an instance do not compile; static methods do not use `this`.

snippet.label: Duplicate parameter names
snippet.explanation: Strict mode rejects duplicate parameter names at parse time. TypeScript also flags duplicate identifiers in signatures.

snippet.label: Modules are always strict
snippet.explanation: ES modules cannot run in sloppy mode. Modern bundlers emit modules or inject strict — treat implicit globals as a legacy script problem.

blocks.title: Safety mechanisms
rows: Compile error if noImplicitAny + proper lint

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Forgetting that `'use strict'` only applies to its function or whole script — a directive inside a block `{ 'use strict'; }` in sloppy scripts does not enable strict for the block (only functions). Assuming TypeScript prevents all sloppy issues — it type-checks, but emitted JS in non-module targets may still allow globals without eslint `no-implicit-globals`. Testing `this` behavior in sloppy REPL then deploying strict bundles. Concatenating third-party sloppy scripts that rely on implicit globals.

interviewTakeaways: Strict mode turns silent failures into throws: implicit globals, bad `delete`, duplicate params, octal literals.
ES modules and class bodies are strict automatically — modern code rarely runs sloppy.
`this` in unbound functions is `undefined` in strict mode, global object in sloppy.
60s: Strict opts into safer rules. Modules always strict. Sloppy allows implicit globals and loose this. C# enforces at compile time what strict catches at run time.
Follow-up: does `'use strict'` inside a block enable strict mode for that block?
commonPitfalls: Believing `'use strict'` in a block scopes strict to that block — only function or script scope works.
Debugging `this` in sloppy REPL then surprised in strict production bundles.
Strong answer: 'Modules strict by default. No implicit globals. this undefined in plain functions. C# catches these at compile.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# rejects undeclared identifiers and duplicate params at compile time. JavaScript strict mode catches some of the same issues at run time — only if strict is enabled.
TypeScript files with `import`/`export` compile to ES modules which are strict. `tsconfig` module setting affects whether emitted code inherits strict-by-default modules.
